paragraphs: In the eleventh year of Jianyuan, the rains came to Chang’an. The market cries could still be heard by day. Toward dusk, clouds bore down from the upper Wei, and the gilded bronze beasts on the palace gates lost their gleam. Thunder split the night. Then rain swept in like an army at full gallop and washed the avenue beyond Vermilion Bird Gate bare.

Before Chengming Hall the lamps burned brightly, yet an unsettling silence prevailed. Water stood deep on the blue-stone steps. Palace attendants hurried past bearing bowls of medicine, careful that their boots should make no sound on the wet bricks. Ministers in purple robes and generals in armor lined the two sides of the entrance. Some had waited half the night, hiding even their coughs in their sleeves.
The man lying within was Wang Meng.

For more than a decade, whenever Fu Jian could not decide how troops should be dispatched from Guanzhong, how taxes should be levied in the prefectures, or which commanders should remain in the conquered cities of Hebei, he would ask what Jinglüe thought. A word from Wang Meng could ruin a great house overnight or turn an army around a thousand miles away. The realm seemed to continue as before, but countless men were already calculating who would hold power in Chang’an tomorrow if he closed his eyes tonight.

Murong Chui stood in the shadow of a corridor pillar. Rain soaked the shoulders of his black cloak, but he made no move to shelter himself. His weapons had been taken at the palace gate. Now and then his hand dropped, from long habit, toward the sword at his waist; finding only an empty belt, it stopped.
“I fear Lord Wang will not survive this,” someone beside him said.
Yao Chang spoke gently, with some of the weariness of a long ride still on his face. He glanced toward the hall as though by chance, then bent to brush the water from the edge of his boot.
“The imperial physicians have yet to come out,” Murong Chui replied.
“I was not speaking of his illness.”
Murong Chui turned to look at him.
Yao Chang smiled. “While the Grand Commandant lives, there is always someone to advise the Heavenly King against taking up arms. Who will do it afterward?”
“There are ministers enough at court.”
“Ministers have voices. Not all of them have courage.”

A gust rushed down the corridor, bending every lamp flame backward. For a moment the two men looked at each other through the sound of rain. Neither continued. Murong Chui understood. Fu Jian held most of the northern lands, with men of many peoples serving beneath his banners. Yet beyond the Yangtze, the Jin court still raised its own standard. So long as it flew, the emperor would never sleep entirely at ease.
A sudden cough came from inside the hall.

The coughing grew sharper, as if some heavy thing were struggling to break free of the chest that held it. Yao Chang lifted his head; Murong Chui straightened. Dozens of eyes fixed on the narrow crack of the doorway. Only when the coughing ceased could they hear the rain again.

Chengming Hall was fragrant with imported incense, though the bitter smell of medicine hung around the brazier. Fu Jian sat beside the sickbed without his crown, one sleeve darkened by spilled medicine. He had kept vigil for hours. Several times the attendants had begged him to take food in a side chamber; each time he had waved them away.

Wang Meng had grown so thin that he seemed to have sunk into the embroidered bedding. Fu Jian remembered the scholar’s cottage at Huayin: Wang Meng in rough clothes, proud in bearing, discussing the rise and fall of kingdoms as if the whole world were a game of chess whose end he already knew. Fu Jian had been young then, with more ambition than soldiers. He had listened with shining eyes, eager to draw his sword and win the four seas at once. Wang Meng had merely smiled and told him first to learn how to govern a single county in Guanzhong.
Now Guanzhong, Hebei, and Bashu had fallen one by one to Qin, and the man who had once pointed out the mountains and rivers with a laugh could scarcely lift his hand.
“Jinglüe,” Fu Jian called softly, “the medicine is still warm.”
Wang Meng slowly opened his eyes and glanced at the physicians.
“Leave us. All of you.”
The physicians looked uncertainly at Fu Jian. He made a small motion with his hand. The doors closed, and the rain resumed its close, incessant tapping against the papered windows.
“I know what you mean to tell me.” Fu Jian took a cloth and wiped the medicine from Wang Meng’s lips. “I shall attend to affairs of court. For now, you must recover.”
“Whenever Your Majesty does not wish to hear me, you tell me to recover.”
Fu Jian’s mouth moved, but he could not quite summon a smile.
Wang Meng watched him for a long while. Then he asked, “Do you remember the first meal I served you at Huayin?”
“Half a bowl of millet porridge. So salty I could barely swallow it.”
“I had borrowed the salt.”
“And after all the gold and silks I gave you, you have never once thought those worth mentioning.”

“The gold and silk were Your Majesty’s gifts. The porridge was mine.” His breathing steadied a little. “There was a family below the mountain. The man had gone off with the soldiers, leaving his old mother and two children. That winter they had no grain. They boiled a pot of elm bark. When I went to see them, the younger child asked whether there would be rice to eat next year if they had a different emperor.”
Fu Jian lowered his eyes.
“I had no answer,” Wang Meng went on. “When I met Your Majesty afterward, I thought perhaps I might find one for that child.”
“The people are safer now than they were then.”
“They are. But it is not enough.”

Those three words filled Fu Jian with a sudden foreboding. Wang Meng had never demanded perfection in governing. He knew what could wait, what must be endured, and what had to be cut away at once, even at the cost of his reputation. If he said it was not enough, he had seen some fracture Fu Jian had failed to see.
“Then speak,” Fu Jian said. “Tonight I will listen.”

Wang Meng did not answer at once. His eyes passed beyond Fu Jian to the map hanging in the hall. It had once been a modest sheet of silk, but new prefectures had been added year after year; twice, more fabric had been sewn to its edges. Whenever another stretch of land was colored in, Fu Jian summoned him to see it. The last time had been the night news came of victory in Bashu. Holding a lamp before the map, the emperor had pointed to the southern hills and rivers still unmarked by Qin’s color and asked how much longer the lands south of the Yangtze must wait.
“When I am dead, Your Majesty will march against Jin,” Wang Meng said.
Fu Jian’s hand grew still on the edge of the bed.
“I have told you before. The realm cannot remain divided forever.”
“And I urged Your Majesty to defeat Yan and secure Shu. Those lands are ours now, yet I beg you not to march south. Do you know why?”
“Because you fear defeat.”
“I fear victory more.”
Fu Jian stared at him.

Wang Meng paused to catch his breath. “If Jiangnan could be taken in a single campaign, Your Majesty would trust all the more in Heaven’s favor. Suppose Qin’s armies swept into Jiankang and every commandery lay within the same borders. Who would still dare tell you that the Yan people of Hebei obey only Yan commanders, that the Qiang tribes keep oaths of their own, that the grain recorded in the prefectural granaries bears little relation to what grows in the fields?”
“I ordered the Department of State Affairs to inspect those accounts every year.”

“It has inspected them. The reports look handsome enough.” Wang Meng gave a bitter smile. “Last month I met grain porters from Hedong. Ten men set out with one wagon. By the time it reached the Luo River, there were only seven. The other three had died, but their names were never entered among the dead. Read only the accounts and you would think all ten had returned home.”
Fu Jian frowned. “Why did you not report this sooner?”
“I did. Your Majesty was debating the southern campaign that day.”
Silence settled over the hall. Rain struck the half-open lid of a bronze brazier with a faint, uneven patter.

Fu Jian rose and walked toward the map. The territories marked in vermilion ran east to the sea, west into Long and Shu, north beyond the Yellow River. Years of bloodshed and calculation had gone into winning that sweep of mountains and rivers. He reached out toward the Jianghuai region.

“Jinglüe, the Jin court has sheltered in one corner for years. Noble families govern in its name, and its generals pull against one another. If I do not take it now, the opportunity may never return. Is it wrong to want peace for all under Heaven?”
“Peace must come,” Wang Meng said, watching his back. “But is it peace for all under Heaven that Your Majesty desires—or to see all under Heaven subject to Chang’an before your own life ends?”
Fu Jian turned, anger flashing in his eyes.
“You think I cannot set aside that glory?”
“I know how hard it would be for Your Majesty.”

Fu Jian looked at him a long while before sitting again. From anyone else, the accusation would have been insolence. Yet this was the man who had survived the deadly struggles of the Fu clan at his side, who had seen him at his lowest and known the secrets he hid even from himself.
“How many spans of ten years does a man have?” Fu Jian asked.
“Your Majesty has one lifetime. Govern Qin well, and it will have the lifetimes of many generations.”
“And if I never see the realm united?”
“Let the crown prince do it. If he cannot, let his children and grandchildren try.”
Fu Jian laughed suddenly, though there was weariness in it. “So I am to spend my years preparing a road for those who come after me.”
“What ruler has ever done otherwise?”
Fu Jian lowered his head for a long time. “In the end, it is Murong Chui you fear.”
Wang Meng’s eyes sharpened.
“He is hardly the only one.”
“When he came over to us, I raised him with my own hands. He has risked his life for Qin, and still you wanted me to put him to death.”
“I am not asking for his death today. I am asking that you take his former troops out of his hands.”
“Strip a man of command in return for service? Who would ever surrender to Qin again?”
“Give him wealth and honors. Make use of his talents when you need them. But do not allow him to become the master of the Yan people once more.”
“And Yao Chang?”
“Keep him in the capital, away from the Qiang country.”
“Murong Wei?”
“Do not let him return to Ye.”
“The Di armies under our own kinsmen?”
“Reform them too.”
Fu Jian looked up. “You would spare not even our own family?”
“Begin with our own family. Only then will others believe us.”

Lightning flared beyond the window, illuminating Wang Meng’s ashen face. Fu Jian remembered how, when Wang Meng first set about restoring order to Guanzhong, his bitterest enemies had been members of the Fu clan and the veterans who had helped place Fu Jian on the throne. Petitioners came in their dozens begging for pardons. Wang Meng instead laid file after file before the emperor, demanding that he choose between old attachments and the law. Fu Jian had cursed his severity more than once. Later he had understood: Guanzhong was what it had become because one man had been willing to undertake such thankless work.
“Jinglüe,” he said softly, “even dying, you refuse to leave me a moment’s peace.”
“When Your Majesty asked me to leave the mountains, you promised me a well-governed age. You did not promise me peace and quiet.”
Fu Jian returned to the bedside and straightened the crooked pillow. Wang Meng’s hand was little more than bone, but he managed to catch the emperor’s sleeve.
“Promise me three more things.”
“Name them.”
“For ten years, do not launch an empire-wide war against Jin.”
Fu Jian closed his eyes for a moment.
“The second?”

“Begin reorganizing the armies around the capital. Examine the tiger tallies, the muster rolls, the grain accounts—one by one. Let the soldiers learn to obey the court’s orders, not merely the names of their commanders. I cannot claim to know every part of how it should be done. Those who remain in office must work it out.”
Fu Jian nodded. “And the third?”
“Let Hong begin to share in governing. Your Majesty has fought for so many years, yet all matters of consequence still wait upon a word from your mouth. Chang’an cannot go on waiting forever.”
“He is still young.”
“Your Majesty was younger when you first took up arms.”

Fu Jian began to speak and stopped. He had spent years in the saddle and cherished Fu Hong like a treasure in his palm, always imagining that he could shield his son from the storms a little longer. On this night of all nights Wang Meng was pushing open the door Fu Jian had least wished to face.
“Ten years,” Fu Jian repeated slowly. “Do you know how many at court will curse you if I make that promise?”
“Did they curse me any less while I was alive?”
“They will not even let you rest after death.”
“Then let them say what they like.”
Fu Jian finally laughed, and his eyes filled with tears.

Footsteps sounded abruptly beyond the doors. Before a chamberlain could announce him, Fu Rong’s voice came through the rain: “Your Majesty! An urgent dispatch from Ye—eight hundred li by express courier!”
Fu Jian went himself to open the doors.

Fu Rong entered dripping rainwater, sheltering beneath his robes a military dispatch whose wax seal had already been broken. Seeing Wang Meng still awake, he hesitated, then bowed his head and reported: hidden weapons and armor had been discovered outside Ye, along with a register of former Yan military households—more than thirty-seven hundred of them. Certain men were said to have entered a secret compact to rise when Qin’s armies marched south and left Hebei undefended. The leaders had not been identified; the testimony itself still required verification.

Fu Jian brought the dispatch to the lamp. A smear of mud marked one corner, with a blade of wet grass caught in the fold. Names crowded the page. Some belonged to the Murong clan; many did not. More than thirty-seven hundred households: to punish them all together would mean tens of thousands of lives.
“Is Murong Chui implicated?” Fu Jian asked.
“There is no evidence as yet.”

“Remember those words.” Fu Jian handed the dispatch back. “Without evidence, no one is to arrest a Yan official residing in the capital. Investigate the weapons and the messengers thoroughly. Show no indulgence, but allow no man to settle a private grudge under cover of this affair.”
Fu Rong acknowledged the order but did not leave. Both brothers knew that if news of the army reforms escaped tonight, Hebei would grow suspicious, and men in Chang’an would grow resentful.

Fu Jian turned back to Wang Meng. The sick man’s eyes were half closed; he might have been asleep. But Fu Jian knew he was waiting, as he had waited for more than ten years, for his sovereign to decide among a thousand hazards what no one else could decide for him.

“Summon Quan Yi, Zhu Rong, and the crown prince,” Fu Jian ordered. “The Feathered Forest Guard will take charge of every gate. Any minister who entered the palace tonight shall remain within it until an edict permits him to leave.”
Fu Rong started. “Elder Brother, Murong Chui and Yao Chang are both waiting in the corridor.”
“Let them wait.”
“And our kinsmen among the generals?”
“The same.”

Fu Rong watched his elder brother and suddenly saw the man who had once gathered heroes around him by sheer force of spirit thrusting his hand into a blazing furnace to draw out a piece of iron not yet forged. If he mishandled it, he would be the first to burn.
“There may be chaos in the capital by morning.”
“Then see that the palace gates are secure tonight.”
Fu Rong withdrew to carry out the order. As the doors closed, the rattle of armor sounded in the distance: the palace guard was changing posts.
Fu Jian sat beside the bed again.
“Jinglüe. The three things you asked of me—I agree.”
Wang Meng did not open his eyes, but his lips moved. “Your Majesty, spoken promises leave no proof.”
“You would have me put it in writing?”
“I would.”

Fu Jian ordered edict paper brought in. He spread it across the writing table and ground the ink himself. He had written orders without number in his lifetime, yet now he held the brush suspended for a long while. Storm and darkness pressed against the windows. Outside stood old courtiers, surrendered generals, and royal kinsmen, each with his own calculations. On the other side of the table Wang Meng’s breathing had grown so faint it was almost lost beneath the rain.

Fu Jian wrote the first command: for ten years there would be no all-out southern campaign. The second ordered a review of the army registers. Former commanders would retain custody of their troops until the Department of State Affairs and the Central Army Office devised a workable system of reassignment. The third instructed Crown Prince Fu Hong to attend the Department of State Affairs and learn the work of government, beginning with soldiers' pay, land taxes, and appointments to office.
When he had finished, he put down the brush. His knuckles were white from gripping it.
“Everything I promised you is here. But you must promise me one thing in return.”
“Tell me, Your Majesty.”
“Live through the night.”
Wang Meng slowly opened his eyes.

“Tomorrow there will be a hall full of men to argue with you. Quan Yi will bring out the old ledgers; Fu Rong will say we are moving too quickly; and Murong Chui will hardly hand over his tiger tally without a word. I cannot quarrel with them all by myself.”
A faint, indistinct laugh escaped Wang Meng’s throat. Moisture gathered at the corners of his eyes.
“I shall do my best.”

Fu Jian bent and enclosed the other man’s hand in both his own. The hand that had once held a brush and determined men’s lives was as light as a withered twig. He turned his face toward the shadows, and it was a long time before he dared look back.

Outside, soldiers of the Feathered Forest Guard hurried along the galleries with torches raised. Iron locks fell one after another upon the palace gates, their heavy clang passing through curtain after curtain of rain. Murong Chui glanced at the newly posted sentries, and his right hand strayed again to his swordless waist. Beside him Yao Chang still wore a smile, but he had not spoken for a very long time.
No one in Chang’an yet knew how many lives that night would change.

The lamps of Chengming Hall burned on. Three edicts, their ink still damp, lay beneath a paperweight, the scent of fresh writing mingling with the bitterness of medicine. Wang Meng drifted in and out of consciousness while Fu Jian kept watch beside the desk, listening as the rain slackened, then began again beneath the eaves.
The Fei River was a thousand li away. That night, the emperor finally agreed to let it remain so for another ten years.
